items.context: 德國法蘭克福機場兩名地勤人員感染瘧疾身亡，官方研判病媒蚊是搭飛機入境的。另外還有四名員工確診住院，機場已在周邊布設捕蚊陷阱。

sources.summary: An adaptation of Peter Heller’s 2012 novel never finds its footing with overly familiar survival beats and a glum lack of energy Looking towards the end of an August movie dumping ground littered with more unwanted trash than usual, there seemed to be a faint glimmer of hope, a shiny treasure poking out through the dusty mass of unnecessary sequels and sex purge romcoms . Somehow, there was a $110m-budget adaptation of an acclaimed novel directed by Ridley Scott, led by a recently Oscar-nominated rising star with support from two Oscar-nominated actors and an Oscar winner. But why then would such a film be unveiled in between the summer blockbuster season and the upcoming deluge of prestige fall festival big hitters? A cursed weekend that’s recently been home to Jay Roach’s heinous War of the Roses remake, Dennis Quaid’s Ronald Reagan biopic and George Miller’s hard-to-define and even harder-to-love flop Three Thousand Years of Longing. Ever since The Dog Stars, based on Peter Heller’s 2012 novel, had been yanked from its far more encouraging date at the end of March, there were multiple red flags flying and the rotten end of August has ultimately become an appropriate punishment for a limp and lethargic film that only briefly fascinates in pushing us to wonder what anyone was really hoping this would end up being. It’s yet another grubby postapocalyptic survival tale, an overcrowded subgenre that hasn’t just reached maximum capacity on the big screen but on the small one too. In a world of seven Walking Dead shows, the beats are now far too familiar – artfully dishevelled actors grieve for the past and fear for the future as they scramble to find and protect resources – and there’s nothing new or notable here to conjure anything but deja vu. sources.summary: With their twangy sound, madcap outfits, lusty yodelling and pirouetting pirate frontman, the band became global superstars almost overnight. But, as their guitarist Marco Pirroni recalls, the thrill ride soon hit the buffers ‘The essence of pop is, one, brilliant fucking songs – and the rest is sex, subversion, style and humour. And that was us .” So Adam Ant told me in 1995, describing the reconstructed Adam and the Ants, which formed in early 1980 with the arrival of guitarist/songwriter Marco Pirroni, who was sitting next to him. “We’re responsible for bringing back dressing up, going mad and screaming your head off.” “That’s it!” grins Pirroni when I remind him of this, as we sit in the shabby-chic lounge of London’s 21Soho venue. Back then, I didn’t tell them I was 15 in 1980, forever sprinting across dancefloors pretending to be Adam Ant, chiffon scarves tied to knees, limbs flailing like a whirling Cossack. Pirroni hears this today and laughs. “That’s what it’s all about,” he hoots. “When I was 13, watching Bowie, Roxy, T Rex, you just go, ‘I wanna do that.’ It’s exciting, sexy, about looking good, Top of the Pops. I can’t imagine anyone saying, ‘Wow, I desperately want to be in Cabaret Voltaire. They must be earning no money, look boring and nobody likes them – that’s the band for me!’” Continue reading...

sources.summary: Pleasance Dome, Edinburgh This show about Olesker’s lengthy journey to becoming an Orthodox Jew in order to marry his partner is both elegant and nuanced ‘I would do anything for love,” Meat Loaf sang, “but I won’t do that.” Max Olesker would, if his solo show Making the Cut – based on his memoir – is any guide. It recounts the comic and writer’s conversion from liberal to Orthodox Judaism, a process required so he can marry his sweetheart – but which, in the meantime, forbids him from so much as touching her for years on end, and forbids much else besides. Secularists may be left reeling. Olesker himself clearly has deeply ambivalent feelings about what he’s gone through. That all makes for a gripping story, of course, that begins when this former half of Max and Ivan meets his dream woman at the Edinburgh fringe. He’s Jewish, she’s Jewish: what’s the problem? It’s that the Olesker family’s loose-fitting and bohemian religious tradition is not considered Jewish by his fiancee’s. If love’s young dream is to be fulfilled, Max must renounce his name, foreswear his profession, keep his hands off his fiancee, visit synagogue three times a day in seeming perpetuity – oh, and get circumcised, too. (Who said romance was dead?) Continue reading...

sources.summary: Beneath the wig and rhinestones, Parton was the genius behind strings of classic songs from Jolene to I Will Always Love You that continue to inspire new artists Dolly Parton, US country star, actor and philanthropist, dies aged 80 Dolly Parton’s family say goodbye to their aunt, sister, grandmother - video Share your tributes and memories of Dolly Parton In December 1977, Dolly Parton submitted to an interview with ABC Television’s Barbara Walters, much against her friends’ advice. Walters was not noted for her deep love and understanding of country music. She was a notoriously tough cookie, a Boston-born, Sarah Lawrence-educated journalist who had battled scarcely believable sexism to become the first female co-host of an American news programme. The month before she met Parton, she had interviewed Anwar Sadat and Menachem Begin while they were working out the terms of the Egypt-Israel peace treaty. It was all a very long way from Parton’s world, and the interview has something of the anthropological exercise about it. Walters looks aghast as Parton shows her around her tour bus, her collection of wigs and her “hand-washable and wrinkle-free” stage outfits (“you really like this? To me, it seems like horror”), and sits impassively as Parton sings Coat of Many Colours to her: an impressive feat, given the song’s saga of rural poverty and homespun wisdom is the mother of all tearjerkers from an artist never averse to yanking at her audience’s heartstrings. She asks Parton if people from “where I come from” would call her a hillbilly; regards the singer’s outfit with a jaundiced eye and tells her “you don’t have to look like this”. And, most infamously, she enquires: “Do you ever feel that you’re a joke?” Continue reading...

sources.summary: Parton put her millions behind causes she believed in – from Covid vaccines to the Imagination Library, which sends children around the world a free book every month Dolly Parton dies aged 80 | Celebrity tributes | A life in pictures Parton’s peerless career turned country music cliches inside out Share your tributes and memories of Dolly Parton In 1991, Dolly Parton made an startling offer to every seventh and eighth-grade student in Sevier County, Tennessee where she grew up: the world-famous singer would personally give them $500 each if they graduated high school. The children had to pick a buddy to hold each other accountable; if one didn’t graduate, the other wouldn’t get the cash. But the idea worked: the county’s high school dropout rate plummeted from 35% to 6%. This was the sort of practical, radical act of charity that Parton, nicknamed “St Dolly”, dedicated her life to trying out. By showing that all it took was the promise of $500 to incentivise kids to stay at school, Sevier County had to address the drop out rate (and it did). It is telling that the tributes shared after Parton’s death at 80 have been equally about her philanthropy and her music. There was so much of both. She told People in 2021: “I’m kind of addicted to the feeling of giving. Knowing that I’m doing something good for someone else.” Continue reading...

items.context: 台北市政府接獲統健公司通報，「麻油車頂級冷壓黑麻油」檢驗出苯駢芘超標，衛生局已要求預防性下架 187 瓶，不分批號。主要通路聖德科斯也開放退費，後續將擴大抽驗黑麻油、花生油、葵花油與棕櫚油等油品。
items.thread_text: 公視報導，台北市政府接獲統健公司通報，「麻油車頂級冷壓黑麻油」檢驗出苯駢芘超標。北市衛生局已要求不分批號，預防性下架 187 瓶，主要通路聖德科斯同步開放退費，後續將擴大抽驗黑麻油、花生油、葵花油與棕櫚油等油品。
items.threads_text: 公視報導，台北市政府接獲統健公司自主通報，指向統購公司購買的「麻油車頂級冷壓黑麻油」檢驗出苯駢芘超標。北市衛生局已要求不分批號，預防性下架 187 瓶，主要通路聖德科斯同步開放退費。後續衛生局將針對黑麻油、花生油、葵花油與棕櫚油等油品，進行擴大抽驗，避免類似狀況再發生。
items.voice_text: 這則跟台灣有關。台北市有一款「麻油車頂級冷壓黑麻油」，被檢出苯駢芘超標。市府已經要求預防性下架，不分批號，一共下架一百八十七瓶。主要通路聖德科斯也開放退費，接下來還會擴大抽驗黑麻油、花生油、葵花油和棕櫚油這些油品。
